scenario: A 72-year-old woman with COPD who uses a long-acting beta-agonist and an inhaled corticosteroid comes to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening dyspnea and productive cough. On arrival, respiratory rate is 28/min, oxygen saturation is 88% on room air, and she has diffuse wheezing. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation without infiltrate, pneumothorax, or pulmonary edema. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.32, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, PaO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L. Over the next hour she receives three nebulized albuterol-ipratropium treatments, oral prednisone 40 mg, and controlled oxygen by Venturi mask titrated to SpO2 90%. She remains alert and oriented, can clear her secretions, and has blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg and heart rate 104/min, but her respiratory rate is now 28/min with accessory muscle use. Repeat arterial blood gas on oxygen shows pH 7.29, PaCO2 65 mm Hg, PaO2 62 mm Hg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Repeat nebulized albuterol and ipratropium and recheck the blood gas in 1 hour
Increase supplemental oxygen to keep SpO2 above 96%

scenario: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after the sudden onset of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm that began while he was gardening. Perform emergency coronary angiography with primary PCI
